content: Toxic multinodular goiter (TMNG) arises due to hyperfunctioning thyroid follicles that produce an excessive amount of thyroid hormones. This condition typically develops in a thyroid gland that has undergone hypertrophy as a result of prolonged stimulation, often due to iodine deficiency or other causes of primary hypothyroidism. When levels of T3 and T4 are low, the thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) is persistently elevated, leading to hypertrophy of the thyroid gland and the development of either focal or diffuse hyperplasia. Some nodules within the thyroid may undergo hyperplasia and develop autonomous activity, while others may degenerate, bleed, or calcify. Once the thyroid gland experiences global activation and hyperplasia, thyrotoxicosis can occur. This is driven by focal proliferation of epithelial cells and the secretion of thyroxine. Hyperplastic thyroid glands are more prone to developing toxic goiter due to several factors. For instance, the high proliferation rate in hyperplastic glands can result in unchecked transcription errors, which may lead to various mutations, including those that activate cyclic AMP (cAMP) pathways, such as TSH receptor (TSH-R) and Gsα mutations. The synthesis of thyroxine involves the production of hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) and other free radicals, which increases the likelihood of mutations. Additionally, a thyroid gland under the stress of excessive proliferation—induced by hypothyroidism and prolonged TSH stimulation—exhibits increased expression of growth factors. Even after the initial stimulus resolves, the proliferating follicles may continue to produce thyroxine independently of TSH stimulation. Furthermore, cells harboring mutations will continue to propagate, producing more cells with the same mutations. Historically, goiter was first observed in the inhabitants of the Alps, who noted that consuming seaweed improved the condition, supporting the theory that iodine deficiency was the underlying cause. Goiter was also described in Ancient Greece, where it was referred to as bronchocele, approximately 200 years before the thyroid gland was discovered. By 1850, iodine consumption was proposed as a preventive measure for goiter, leading to the inclusion of iodine in meals provided to students. In 1884, thyroidectomies were successfully performed as a treatment for goiter. However, in the 19th century, the mortality rate for thyroidectomies performed by Kocher was reported to be 5%. Goiters can be classified into several types. A diffuse goiter refers to a goiter that affects the entire thyroid gland and can be further categorized as either a simple goiter or a multinodular goiter. A toxic goiter is associated with hyperthyroidism and is most commonly caused by Graves' disease, though it can also result from inflammation or multinodular goiter. In contrast, a nontoxic goiter is associated with normal or low thyroid hormone levels and includes goiters caused by factors such as lithium use or certain autoimmune diseases.
